title: When the saints go marching in
word: When the saints go marching in
hook: spirituals turned Revelation into hope: wanting to be in that number

segments.voice: Yesterday, Revelation in wool and woodcut, every picture a reading. Your line was art unveils. What did the picture you looked at uncover? Day one thousand three hundred nineteen.

A brass band starts up on a street. A trombone slides, a drum kicks in, and people who were only watching start falling in behind. The tune is When the Saints Go Marching In. It's sung slow in churches and played fast by bands, and nobody can say for certain who first sang it. Under the bounce there's one plain wish. When the saints go marching in on the last day, the singer wants to be in that number. Counted. Not watching from the curb. Some listeners hear that number in the seventh chapter of Revelation, and that's where this lesson goes.

First, the number John hears. "And I heard the number of them which were sealed: and there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand of all the tribes of the children of Israel." A precise count, tribe by tribe. Second, what John sees when he looks up: "After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands." He hears a number, then sees a crowd nobody can count. Christians explain the two pictures in different ways: as two groups, or as one people seen two ways. And if the song's that number is this crowd, it's a number nobody can count. Third, who they are. An elder tells John: "These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb." People who came through hard things. And the chapter ends with a line this block has met before: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." Fourth, who counts as a saint. In Paul's letters the word means the members of a church. He writes "to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi." Catholic and Orthodox Christians, and some Protestants, also honor particular saints by name, with feast days; other Protestants keep the word mostly for the whole church. Either way, the song isn't about a few famous names. Other spirituals sing Bible pictures as present hope too: a chariot swinging low, a balm in Gilead. This one takes a crowd before the throne and puts the singer in it.

Here's the practice: sing the song. If you know it, sing it or hum it softly, and slowly, more like a hymn than a parade. If you don't, hum any tune you love. Settle, and breathe between the lines. As you go, bring to mind the people you'd want in that number with you: someone who taught you, someone who came through something hard, someone you've lost. Let the crowd grow in your mind past what you can count. If you pray, you can hold them before God. If you don't, just sing them in. The bell holds the time.
When the saints go marching in. A song with one wish, to be counted among the saints, and, some hear, Revelation's multitude which no man could number.

howItsDone: When the Saints Go Marching In is sung in some churches and played by brass bands, including at funerals in New Orleans, and some churches read Revelation 7:9–17 on All Saints' Day.

what a scholar hears: Revelation 7:9, the multitude "which no man could number", right after the counted sealed of 7:4; readers differ on how the two pictures fit.

notes: No song lyrics are quoted; the refrain is paraphrased ('the singer wants to be in that number'), and the carry 'in that number' is the index's.

The song's origin is described only as uncertain ('nobody can say for certain who first sang it'). It is usually called a traditional spiritual or gospel song; the link to Revelation 7 is presented as the lesson's reading. Confirm.
Spirituals named by image only (Swing Low, Sweet Chariot; There Is a Balm in Gilead), not quoted. Confirm the description 'Bible pictures sung as present hope'.
Two readings of the 144,000 and the multitude (two groups; one people seen two ways) given unranked. Confirm.
'Protestants tend to use the word for the whole church' and Catholic/Orthodox veneration of named saints: confirm the wording is fair.
howItsDone mentions New Orleans funeral bands and All Saints' Day readings; confirm.
